claim: Eighty-six participants took part in this experiment, comprising 20 patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), 12 patients with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and 54 healthy control participants.
source: Eighty-six participants took part in this experiment, comprising 20patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), 12patients with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and 54 healthy control participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant composition in the study.

claim: Patients with MDD and GAD achieved a significantly lower hit rate compared to healthy controls.
source: Patients with MDD and GAD exhibit three key behavioral patterns as compared to healthy controls. First, patients achieved a significantly lower hit rate (averaged across stable and volatile contexts) as compared to the healthy controls (Figure 2A; t(70.541) = 3.326, p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.723).
evidence: Statistical test results (t-test with p=0.001) support this claim, and Figure 2A provides visual evidence.

claim: Patients' learning curves took more trials to converge to an asymptote, indicating seemingly slower learning.
source: Second, we observed two atypical features of learning curves in the patient group (Figure 2B). The patients' learning curves took more trials to converge to an asymptote (i.e. seemingly slower learning).
evidence: Direct observation from learning curve analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a larger apparent deviation from the true feedback probability in the patient group.
source: Additionally, there was a larger apparent deviation (Figure 2B, blue arrows) from the true feedback probability. The apparent deviation indicates that the learning curve of the patient group could never converge to the true feedback probability, even given a sufficient number of trials in a stable context.
evidence: Visual evidence from Figure 2B showing deviation marked by blue arrows.

claim: The patient group showed a reduced hit rate difference between volatile and stable contexts.
source: Third, aside from the lower learning rate and atypical learning curves that indicate inferior performance in the patient group, we further discovered a reduced hit rate difference within the patient group (Figure 2 and t(55.648) = 2.038, p = 0.046, Cohen's d = 0.478).
evidence: Statistical test results (t-test with p=0.046) and Figure 2 support this finding.

claim: Hit rate difference is marginally associated with the severity of participants' symptoms.
source: Interestingly, this hit rate difference is marginally associated with the severity of participants' symptoms (r(86) = –0.194, p = 0.074), as measured using the bifactor analysis reported in Gagne et al., 2020.
evidence: Correlation analysis with p=0.074 (marginal significance) and citation to Gagne et al., 2020.

claim: MOS6 and MOS22 were the best-fitting models in terms of BIC and AIC, respectively.
source: MOS6 and MOS22 were the best-fitting models in terms of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978) and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974), respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: Model comparison results shown in Figure 3A with citations to BIC and AIC criteria.

claim: Group-level Bayesian model comparison supports MOS6 as the best-fitting model.
source: The group-level Bayesian model comparison (Rigoux et al., 2014) further supports MOS6 as the best-fitting model (Figure 3B).
evidence: Bayesian model comparison results shown in Figure 3B with citation to Rigoux et al., 2014.

claim: No group differences in learning rate were found in the MOS6 model.
source: Most importantly, we also examined the learning rate parameter in the MOS6 but found no group differences (t(68.692) = 0.690, p = 0.493, Cohen's d = 0.151).
evidence: Statistical test results (t-test with p=0.493, non-significant) showing no learning rate differences.

claim: The EU strategy achieved the highest hit rate among the three strategies.
source: For hit rate, our simulations showed that the EU strategy achieved the highest hit rate, while the MO strategy basically performed at the chancel-level (Figure 4B).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 4B demonstrating EU strategy performance.

claim: The MO strategy performed at chance-level for hit rate.
source: For hit rate, our simulations showed that the EU strategy achieved the highest hit rate, while the MO strategy basically performed at the chancel-level (Figure 4B).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 4B demonstrating MO strategy performance.

claim: The HA strategy achieved an above-chance hit rate.
source: Interestingly, our simulations also showed that the HA strategy achieved an above-chance hit rate. This is because, although the HA strategy appears not to consider feedback probability directly, it still somewhat tracks feedback probability by simply repeating the past choices made by the EU.
evidence: Simulation results with explanation of mechanism.

claim: Patients with severe symptoms exhibit a weaker preference for the cognitively demanding EU strategy.
source: Our findings indicate that patients with severe symptoms exhibit a weaker preference for the cognitively demanding EU strategy (Pearson's r = –0.221, p = 0.040)
evidence: Correlation analysis with p=0.040 showing relationship between symptom severity and EU preference.

claim: Patients with severe symptoms show a stronger preference for the simpler MO strategy.
source: and a stronger preference for the simpler MO strategy (Pearson's r = 0.360, p = 0.001).
evidence: Correlation analysis with p=0.001 showing relationship between symptom severity and MO preference.

claim: There was a significant correlation between symptom severity and the preference for the HA strategy.
source: Additionally, there was a significant correlation between symptom severity and the preference for the HA strategy (Pearson's r = –0.285, p = 0.007).
evidence: Correlation analysis with p=0.007 showing relationship between symptom severity and HA preference.

claim: No significant correlation was found between learning rate adaptation and symptom severity within the MOS22 model.
source: For completeness, we examined the correlation between learning rate adaptation (log volatile learning rate – log stable learning rate) and symptom severity within the MOS22 model (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Not surprisingly, we found no significant correlation (r(86) = 0.130, p = 0.233)
evidence: Correlation analysis with p=0.233 (non-significant) shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The MOS22 model revealed no learning rate adaptation effect, as indicated by learning rate parameters in the volatile context not being significantly larger than in the stable context.
source: Most importantly, the MOS22 model revealed no learning rate adaptation effect, as indicated by the learning rate parameters in the volatile context not being significantly larger than that in the stable context (F(1, 77) = 0.126, p = 0.724, ƞ2<0.001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: ANOVA results with p=0.724 (non-significant) shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Simulated data generated by MOS6 reproduced the slower learning curve and the apparent difference in the patient group.
source: We simulated each group 20 times, and the simulated data reproduced the slower learning curve and the apparent difference in the patient group (Figure 6A).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 6A demonstrating model's ability to reproduce behavioral patterns.

claim: When FLR22 was fit to simulated data from MOS6, significant differences in learning rate between stable and volatile contexts were found.
source: We fit the simulated data generated by MOS6 with the FLR22 model and found significant differences in the (log) learning rate between stable and volatile contexts (paired t-test(39 ) = –3.217, p = 0.003, Cohen's d = 0.721; Figure 6B).
evidence: Statistical test results (paired t-test with p=0.003) on simulated data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The agent resembling the patient group demonstrated a trend toward reduced learning rate adaptation compared to the agent resembling the healthy control group.
source: Furthermore, the agent resembling the patient group demonstrated a trend toward reduced learning rate adaptation compared to the agent resembling the healthy control group (Figure 6C), consistent with the learning rate adaptation theory.
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 6C demonstrating trend in synthetic data.

claim: Parameter recovery results demonstrate that the true parameters can be accurately estimated and identified in the MOS6 model.
source: The parameter recovery results (Figure 7A) demonstrate that the true parameters can be accurately estimated and identified (all Pearson's rs >0.720)
evidence: Parameter recovery analysis results shown in Figure 7A with correlation values.

claim: In model recovery analysis, the best-fitting model was always the one that generated the data.
source: We then fit all eight models to every dataset using the MAP method as the same before. The best-fitting model was always the one that generated the data, as indicated by all three quantitative metrics: AIC, BIC, and PXP (Figure 7B).
evidence: Model recovery analysis results shown in Figure 7B using multiple metrics.

claim: The MOS and FLR models cannot adequately account for each other's synthetic datasets.
source: Most importantly, the MOS and FLR models cannot adequately account for each other's synthetic datasets, strongly supporting the independent computational effects of strategy preference and learning rate.
evidence: Model recovery analysis demonstrating model distinguishability.

claim: In the volatile reversal learning task, participants chose between two shaped stimuli to receive feedback.
source: In a volatile reversal learning task, participants chose between two shaped stimuli to receive feedback.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental task.

claim: Participants received the presented feedback when choosing the feedback stimulus; otherwise, they received '0'.
source: Participants received the presented feedback (e.g. '27' on the 'square') when choosing the feedback stimulus; otherwise, they received '0' (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct description of task feedback structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The task was divided into four contexts: reward or aversive feedback types crossed with stable or volatile conditions.
source: The task was divided into four contexts: reward or aversive feedback types crossed with stable or volatile conditions.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design.

claim: In stable conditions, one stimulus had a higher fixed feedback probability of 75%.
source: In stable, one stimulus had a higher fixed feedback probability (always 75%)
evidence: Direct description of stable condition parameters.

claim: In volatile conditions, the dominant stimulus switched every 20 trials with probabilities of either 20% or 80%.
source: while in volatile, the dominant stimulus switched every 20 trials (either 20% or 80%), requiring active learning of stimulus-feedback contingencies (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct description of volatile condition parameters shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each run consisted of 180 trials, with 90 trials in the stable context and 90 in the volatile context.
source: Each run consisted of 180 trials, with 90 trials in the stable context and 90 in the volatile context (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct description of experimental structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No additional hints were provided about the transition from one context to another.
source: No additional hints were provided about the transition from one context to another; therefore, participants needed to infer the current context on their own.
evidence: Direct description of experimental procedure.

claim: The MOS model postulates that behavioral differences across participant groups and stable/volatile contexts arise from different weightings of multiple decision strategies.
source: Our target model family, known as MOS, posits that behavioral differences across the two participant groups and between stable/volatile contexts can be attributed to varying weightings of multiple decision strategies: EU, MO, and HA
evidence: Direct statement of the model's core hypothesis.

claim: The EU strategy yields the maximum amount of reward but consumes considerable cognitive resources.
source: This EU strategy yields the maximum amount of reward, but the utility calculation itself consumes considerable cognitive resources.
evidence: Theoretical statement about the EU strategy's properties.

claim: The MO strategy only considers reward magnitude during the decision process.
source: Alternatively, humans may choose simpler strategies, e.g., the magnitude-oriented (MO) strategy, in which only the reward magnitude was considered during the decision process
evidence: Direct definition of the MO strategy.

claim: The HA strategy involves simply repeating decisions frequently made in the past regardless of reward magnitude.
source: and the habitual (HA) strategy, in which people simply repeat decisions frequently made in the past regardless of reward magnitude (Wood and Rünger, 2016).
evidence: Direct definition of the HA strategy with citation to Wood and Rünger, 2016.

claim: Previous studies have identified that individuals with anxiety or depression exhibit a reduced learning rate compared to healthy subjects.
source: Previous studies on reinforcement learning have identified three prominent phenomena: (1) individuals with anxiety or depression exhibit a reduced learning rate compared to healthy subjects
evidence: Summary of prior research findings.

claim: Learning rates may increase or decrease in environments with rapidly changing or stable feedback conditions, a phenomenon termed learning rate adaptation.
source: (2) learning rates may increase or decrease in environments with rapidly changing (i.e. volatile) or stable feedback conditions, a phenomenon termed learning rate adaptation
evidence: Summary of prior research findings defining learning rate adaptation.

claim: Reduced learning rate adaptation is associated with several psychiatric disorders.
source: and (3) reduced learning rate adaptation is associated with several psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Summary of prior research findings.

claim: Human participants are able to flexibly adapt to changes in environmental volatility by increasing and decreasing the learning rate.
source: First, human participants are able to flexibly adapt to changes in environmental volatility, as evidenced by increasing and decreasing the learning rate in response to volatile and stable conditions. This observation is often referred to as the learning rate adaptation effect.
evidence: Summary of prior research findings on learning rate adaptation.

claim: Individuals with several psychiatric disorders, including anxiety and depression, have been found to have a reduced ability to adapt their learning rate in response to environmental volatility.
source: Second, individuals with several psychiatric disorders, including anxiety and depression, have been found to have a reduced ability to adapt their learning rate in response to environmental volatility (Behrens et al., 2007; Browning et al., 2015; Gagne et al., 2020).
evidence: Summary of prior research findings with citations to Behrens et al., 2007; Browning et al., 2015; Gagne et al., 2020.

claim: Reduced learning rate adaptation can be indicative of atypical behaviors.
source: This hallmark can also be indicative of atypical behaviors (Browning et al., 2015; Gagne et al., 2020)
evidence: Summary of prior research with citations to Browning et al., 2015; Gagne et al., 2020.

claim: Reduced learning rate adaptation is associated with psychosis.
source: psychosis (Powers et al., 2017)
evidence: Citation to Powers et al., 2017 linking reduced learning rate adaptation to psychosis.

claim: Reduced learning rate adaptation is associated with autism spectrum disorder.
source: and autism spectrum disorder (Lawson et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to Lawson et al., 2017 linking reduced learning rate adaptation to autism spectrum disorder.

claim: The traditional approach to understanding human behaviors using learning rates increases the number of learning rates as the number of contexts increases, thereby increasing the risk of overfitting.
source: However, the current approach to understanding human behaviors using learning rates has two main limitations. First, the traditional approach increases the number of learning rates as the number of contexts increases, thereby increasing the risk of overfitting.
evidence: Critical analysis of prior methodological approaches.

claim: The traditional learning rate approach implicitly assumes that learning rate differences can account for all behavioral differences between stable/volatile contexts and between healthy controls and patients.
source: Second, this approach implicitly assumes that learning rate differences can account for all behavioral differences between stable/volatile rewarding contexts and group differences between healthy controls and patients with psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Critical analysis of assumptions in prior approaches.

claim: The learning rate is not directly observable and is often estimated by model fitting, which limits its interpretability.
source: However, the learning rate is not directly observable and is often estimated by model fitting, which limits its interpretability.
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations of learning rate estimation.

claim: The MOS model can reproduce three classic phenomena by using a single set of strategy preference parameters without introducing any learning rate differences.
source: Compared to the FLR model, the MOS model can reproduce the three classic phenomena by using a single set of strategy preference parameters without introducing any learning rate differences.
evidence: Summary of model comparison results.

claim: The MOS model can successfully account for several novel behavioral patterns that cannot be explained by the FLR model.
source: In addition, the MOS model can successfully account for several novel behavioral patterns that cannot be explained by the FLR model.
evidence: Summary of model comparison results.

claim: Preferences for different strategies predict individual variations in symptom severity.
source: Preferences for different strategies also predict individual variations in symptom severity.
evidence: Summary of correlation analysis results.

claim: Atypical strategy preference is a potential mechanism for learning deficits in psychiatric disorders.
source: These findings underscore the importance of considering mixed strategy use in human learning and decision-making and suggest atypical strategy preference as a potential mechanism for learning deficits in psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion based on study findings.

claim: The diagnosis was made through a phone screen, an in-person screening session, and the structured clinical interview following DSM-IV-TR (SCID) in 20 MDD patients, 12 GAD patients, and 20 healthy control participants.
source: The diagnosis was made through a phone screen, an in-person screening session, and the structured clinical interview following DSM-IV-TR (SCID) in 20 MDD patients, 12 GAD patients, and 20 healthy control participants.
evidence: Direct description of diagnostic procedures.

claim: The remaining 30 healthy control participants were recruited without SCID.
source: The remaining 30 healthy control participants were recruited without SCID.
evidence: Direct description of recruitment procedures.

claim: The severity of anxiety and depression in all participants was measured by several standard clinical questionnaires.
source: The severity of anxiety and depression in all participants was measured by several standard clinical questionnaires, including the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI form Y; Spielberger et al., 1983), the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI; Beck et al., 1961), the Mood and Anxiety Symptoms Questionnaire (MASQ; Clark and Watson, 1991; Watson and Clark, 1991), the Penn State Worry Questionnaire (Meyer et al., 1990), the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CESD; Radloff, 1977), and the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ; Eysenck and Eysenck, 1975).
evidence: Direct description of clinical assessment methods with citations.

claim: An exploratory bifactor analysis was applied to item-level responses to disentangle variance common to GAD and MDD or unique to each.
source: An exploratory bifactor analysis was then applied to item-level responses in all questionnaires to disentangle the variance that is common to GAD and MDD or unique to each.
evidence: Direct description of statistical analysis method.

claim: The bifactor analysis summarized participants' symptoms into three orthogonal factors: a general factor (g), a depression-specific factor (f1), and an anxiety-specific factor (f2).
source: The results of this analysis summarized participants' symptoms into three orthogonal factors: a general factor (g) explaining the common symptoms, a depression-specific factor (f1), and an anxiety-specific factor (f2), which are all included in the public dataset.
evidence: Direct description of bifactor analysis results.

claim: Participants earned points convertible to monetary rewards in the reward context.
source: Participants earned points, which were convertible to monetary rewards, in the reward context
evidence: Direct description of reward context.

claim: Participants received electric shocks in the aversive context.
source: or received electric shocks in the aversive context.
evidence: Direct description of aversive context.

claim: The reward points in the reward context were converted into a monetary bonus ranging from £0 to £10.
source: The reward points in the reward context were converted into a monetary bonus by the end of the task, ranging from £0 to £10.
evidence: Direct description of reward conversion.

claim: A total of 79 participants completed tasks in both feedback contexts.
source: A total of 79 participants completed tasks in both feedback contexts.
evidence: Direct statement about participant completion rates.

claim: Four participants only completed the task in the reward context.
source: Four participants only completed the task in the reward context
evidence: Direct statement about participant completion rates.

claim: Three participants only completed the aversive task.
source: while three participants only completed the aversive task.
evidence: Direct statement about participant completion rates.

claim: The MOS22 has a total of 22 free parameters.
source: The context-dependent variant MOS22 has a total of 22 free parameters.
evidence: Direct description of model parameters.

claim: Parameters were estimated for each participant via the maximum a posteriori (MAP) method.
source: Parameters were estimated for each participant via the maximum a posteriori (MAP) method.
evidence: Direct description of parameter estimation method.

claim: Parameter estimation was performed using the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm in the scipy.optimize module in Python.
source: Parameter estimation was performed using the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm in the scipy.optimize module in Python.
evidence: Direct description of computational implementation.

claim: For each participant, the optimization was run with 40 randomly chosen initial parameters to avoid local minima.
source: For each participant, we ran the optimization with 40 randomly chosen initial parameters to avoid local minima.
evidence: Direct description of optimization procedure.

source: The data is publicly available via https://osf.io/8mzuj/.
evidence: Direct statement about data availability.
